Module 1 Homework: Chapter 2 Exercises, Problems 8, 9, and 10¶

Ryan Waterman, 7/8/25¶

Problem 8¶

This exercise relates to the College data set, which can be found in the file College.csv on the book website. It contains a number of variables for 777 different universities and colleges in the US. The variables are:

  • Private : Public/private indicator
  • Apps : Number of applications received
  • Accept : Number of applicants accepted
  • Enroll : Number of new students enrolled
  • Top10perc : New students from top 10% of high school class
  • Top25perc : New students from top 25% of high school class
  • F.Undergrad : Number of full-time undergraduates
  • P.Undergrad : Number of part-time undergraduates
  • Outstate : Out-of-state tuition
  • Room.Board : Room and board costs
  • Books : Estimated book costs
  • Personal : Estimated personal spending
  • PhD : Percent of faculty with Ph.D.s
  • Terminal : Percent of faculty with terminal degree
  • S.F.Ratio : Student/faculty ratio
  • perc.alumni : Percent of alumni who donate
  • Expend : Instructional expenditure per student
  • Grad.Rate : Graduation rate

Before reading the data into Python, it can be viewed in Excel or a text editor.

Part B¶

Look at the data used in the notebook by creating and running a new cell with just the code college in it. You should notice that the first column is just the name of each university in a column named something like Unnamed: 0. We don’t really want pandas to treat this as data. However, it may be handy to have these names for later. Try the following commands and similarly look at the resulting data frames:

college2 = pd.read_csv('College.csv', index_col=0) 
college3 = college.rename({'Unnamed: 0': 'College'},
axis=1)
college3 = college3.set_index('College')

This has used the first column in the file as an index for the data frame. This means that pandas has given each row a name corresponding to the appropriate university. Now you should see that the first data column is Private. Note that the names of the colleges appear on the left of the table. We also introduced a new python object above: a dictionary, which is specified by dictionary(key, value) pairs. Keep your modified version of the data with the following:

college = college3

Part H

Continue exploring the data, and provide a brief summary of what you discover.

I am particularly interested in the relationship between expenditure and percentage of faculty with PhDs. Let's explore that relationship.

In [17]:
college.plot.scatter(x='PhD', y='Expend');

Interesting, this is similar to what I was expecting, but I thought the relationship would be more linear. Let's see id the proportion of PhD professors affects graduation rate.

In [18]:
college.plot.scatter(x='PhD', y='Grad.Rate');

Again, this is interesting. There is no visible, meaningful relationship between graduation rate and the proportion of PhD professors. I actually expected this to be slightly inversely proportional because PhD professors typically run labs and perform their own research, so they may be less invested in teaching. I want to explore the effect of out of state tuition on enrollment now.

In [19]:
college.plot.scatter(x='Outstate', y='Enroll');
In [20]:
college.plot.scatter(x='Outstate', y='Top10perc');
In [21]:
college.plot.scatter(x='Outstate', y='Top25perc');
In [22]:
college['Accept.Rate'] = college['Accept']/college['Apps']
In [23]:
college.plot.scatter(x='Outstate', y='Accept.Rate');

There were several trends that I was interested in exploring, and most of them behaved as expected.

  • The first relationship, Outstate vs Enroll, did not show a clear trend. I was expecting this to be negatively correlated, but I didn't adjust for the total number of students at the institution, so this result is conflated with other factors.
  • The second relationship, Outstate vs Top10perc, was moderately positively correlated, which is what I was expecting. As with any product or service, more expensive is generally considered more premium or better, so I expected expensive institutions to attract the best highschool applicants.
  • The third relationship, Outstate vs Top25perc, was also moderatly positively correlated, for the same reason outlined in my Top10perc analysis.
  • The final relationship, Outstate vs Acceptance Rate, was slightly negatively correlated, as expected. The more expensive the institution, the more selective it might be.

Problem 9¶

This exercise involves the Auto data set studied in the lab. Make sure that the missing values have been removed from the data.

In [24]:
# Before getting started, identify and remove the missing data.
# From looking at the csv, I found that horsepower has missing values.
# These are question marks in the dataset, so we will drop that as well.
data_path = './data/Auto.csv'
auto = pd.read_csv(data_path)
auto.dropna(axis=0, how='any')
auto = auto[auto['horsepower'] != '?']
In [25]:
# Origin also needs to be remapped. It is currently using a numerical representation
# to describe the region of origin, which is not ideal. Let's resolve this.

origin_map = {1:'American',
             2:'European',
             3:'Japanese'}

remapped = []

for region in auto['origin']:
    remapped.append(origin_map[region])

auto['origin'] = pd.Series(remapped)

Part A¶

Which of the predictors are quantitative, and which are qualitative?

In [26]:
quantitative = auto.describe().columns
qualitative = [column for column in auto.columns if column not in quantitative]

Out[27]:

Hmmmmm, this doesn't match what I was expecting. Let's look at the type of each column.

In [29]:
for column in auto.columns:
    print(column, auto[column].dtype)

mpg float64
cylinders int64
displacement float64
horsepower object
weight int64

Okay, so here is the root of the issue. Let's go through and change the types of the columns that should be quantitative.

In [30]:
auto['horsepower'] = auto['horsepower'].astype('int64')

There are several interesting trends in these variables. Most notably, displacement vs horsepower, mpg vs weight, and mpg vs year.

  • Displacment vs Horsepower:
    • This is nearly a perfectly linear, positively correlated variable.
  • MPG vs Weight:
    • This appears to have a relationship that resembles exponential decay. MPG is inversely proportional to Weight.
  • MPG vs Year:
    • MPG and Year appear to be moderately positively correlated, which is likely due to design improvements and efficiency regulations.

Part F¶

Suppose that we wish to predict gas mileage (mpg) on the basis of the other variables. Do your plots suggest that any of the other variables might be useful in predicting mpg? Justify your answer.

The plots, above, suggest displacement, horsepower, and weight are strong predictors of gas mileage, while acceleration is a weak predictor. The strong predictors are all negatively correlated with MPG, and each relationship can be categorized as 'exponential decay.' Acceleration time is positively correlated with mpg, which is an intuitive relationship based on how acceleration is correlated with the other factors.

Problem 10¶

This exercise involves the Boston housing data set.

Part A¶

To begin, load in the Boston data set, which is part of the ISLP library.

In [45]:
from ISLP import load_data
In [46]:
boston = load_data('Boston')

Part B¶

How many rows are in this data set? How many columns? What do the rows and columns represent?

In [49]:
boston.info()

From the ISLP website for this dataset (https://intro-stat-learning.github.io/ISLP/datasets/Boston.html)

crim: per capita crime rate by town.

zn: proportion of residential land zoned for lots over 25,000 sq.ft.

indus: proportion of non-retail business acres per town.

chas: Charles River dummy variable (= 1 if tract bounds river; 0 otherwise).

nox: nitrogen oxides concentration (parts per 10 million).

rm: average number of rooms per dwelling.

age: proportion of owner-occupied units built prior to 1940.

dis: weighted mean of distances to five Boston employment centres.

rad: index of accessibility to radial highways.

tax: full-value property-tax rate per $10,000.

ptratio: pupil-teacher ratio by town.

lstat: lower status of the population (percent).

medv: median value of owner-occupied homes in $1000s.

Part C¶

Make some pairwise scatterplots of the predictors (columns) in this data set. Describe your findings.

In [53]:
pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(boston[['dis', 'lstat', 'medv', 'crim']], figsize=(20, 15));

These columns were selected because my hypothesis was the weighted mean of distances to five Boston employment centers would be correlated with the other predictors. I found that there were correlations with the other variables, but not what I expected.

  • Dis vs Lstat:
    • This was negatively, exponentially related. I expected positive, linear correlation.
  • Dis vs Medv:
    • This was positively, logarithmically related. I expected negative, linear correlation.
  • Dis vs Crim:
    • This was negatively, exponentially related. I expected negative, linear correlation.

The key takeaway from my poor assumption is that population density is probably the driving variable.

Part D¶

Are any of the predictors associated with per capita crime rate? If so, explain the relationship.

As seen in the previous scatter matrix, 'dis' is associated with crime rate. My assumption is that 'dis' is actually a strong predictor for population density.

These subrubs appear to be wealthier and safer based on lstat, medv, and crim. Surprisingly, these wealthy suburbs also have some of the lowest tax rates of all suburbs, which is the opposite of what I would expect.
